name: Amcache.hve
os_min: Windows 8 (backported to Windows 7 SP1 via KB2952664)
location: C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve (standalone registry hive, plus Amcache.hve.LOG1/.LOG2 transaction logs in the same folder)
purpose: A registry hive maintained by the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser / Inventory Collector that catalogs executables, installed applications, and loaded drivers seen on the system, recording each file's path, SHA-1 hash, and size. Because the entry is written independently of the file itself, it commonly survives after the underlying binary has been deleted, making it valuable evidence of program presence/first-run even post-deletion.
key_fields: LowerCaseLongPath: full file path of the executable
FileId: a 41-character value: literal prefix "0000" + the SHA-1 hex digest (hashed over roughly the first 31 MiB of the file)
KeyLastWriteTimestamp: registry last-write time of the entry; the closest available proxy for when the entry was first inventoried
LinkDate: PE header compile/link timestamp (attacker-controllable, not a filesystem time)
Publisher / Version / BinFileVersion: PE resource / code-signing metadata
ProgramId: links a file entry (InventoryApplicationFile) to its parent install record (InventoryApplication)
normal_baseline: On Windows 10 1607+ / Windows 11, entries live under Root\InventoryApplicationFile, Root\InventoryApplication, and Root\InventoryDriverBinary inside the hive (older Windows 7 SP1 / Windows 8.x builds instead use a legacy Root\File\{VolumeGUID}\{FileRef} and Root\Programs layout). A clean system accumulates entries for OS binaries, installed applications, and drivers over its lifetime, with plausible LinkDate values consistent with each vendor's known build/release dates and paths under Program Files, Windows, or System32.
anomalies: Executable path under Temp, Downloads, AppData\Local\Temp, ProgramData, or another user-writable/unusual directory with no corresponding InventoryApplication install record
FileId (SHA-1) matches a known-malicious hash, especially when the path is atypical for that hash's known-good usage

Amcache entry exists (proving the file was once present/executed) with no matching file on disk. Evidence of a deleted binary, especially valuable when the same timeframe shows corroborating Prefetch, Shimcache, or BAM entries
LinkDate that postdates KeyLastWriteTimestamp, or is otherwise inconsistent with the rest of the file's metadata. A sign the PE compile timestamp was forged
The same SHA-1 recorded across many hosts under different file names/paths, consistent with a single payload redeployed by an actor
anti_forensic_notes: Deleting the binary from disk does not remove its Amcache record: the inventory snapshot persists in the hive until the next Compatibility Appraiser scheduled-task run, and the prior entry is often still recoverable from the Amcache.hve.LOG1/.LOG2 transaction logs even after that. An investigator who collects only the .hve file (not its .LOG1/.LOG2 companions) on a system that wasn't cleanly shut down can miss the most recent writes. Wiping or replacing Amcache.hve outright, or disabling the Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser task, stops new entries from being recorded going forward but is itself an unusual, noteworthy action to find during triage.
